answer: Interrupted time series (ITS) addresses the maturation threat by fitting separate trend lines before and after an intervention and testing whether the slope changed at the intervention point. Because outcomes may already be moving, ITS compares the post-program slope against a counterfactual that extends the pre-program trend forward. In the tutorial, a county screening program launched in 2019 amid rising rates; when the post-program slope equals the pre-program slope of 2.5% per year, the slope difference is zero and cumulative impact after five and ten years is zero, meaning the program did not accelerate the existing trend.

faqs.q: How does interrupted time series detect a real program effect?
faqs.a: ITS fits a trend line before and after the intervention and asks whether the post-program slope differs meaningfully from the pre-program slope. A slope difference near zero, as in the tutorial, indicates the improvement was already underway.

faqs.q: What is the counterfactual in an interrupted time series design?
faqs.a: The counterfactual is the pre-program trend extended forward as if no program had occurred. The tutorial compares observed post-program data against this no-program projection to isolate any change caused by the intervention.

faqs.q: Why does ITS focus on the slope rather than the level?
faqs.a: Because maturation produces a continuing trend, a higher post-program level can simply reflect that trend continuing. ITS asks whether the rate of change accelerated, so the slope difference, not the level, signals a genuine effect.
